title: Research
text: Many processes follow a known kind of dynamic, such as exponential growth, a burning rate or the course of an epidemic, but real data about them are often sparse, irregular or clustered. Standard curve-fitting methods lose accuracy exactly where the data are thinnest, while fully parametric differential-equation models break down when the assumed equation is only approximately right.

title: Research
text: Many processes follow a known kind of dynamic, such as exponential growth, a burning rate or the course of an epidemic, but real data about them are often sparse, irregular or clustered. Standard curve-fitting methods lose accuracy exactly where the data are thinnest, while fully parametric differential-equation models break down when the assumed equation is only approximately right.

title: Research
text:
My approach
My PhD thesis, Differential Equation-Constrained Local Polynomial Regression Models (UBC Okanagan, 2026; supervisor Dr. W. John Braun), develops a unified framework, DE-LPR, that builds differential-equation information directly into local polynomial regression. The estimator borrows structure from the equation where data are scarce and stays flexible where they are plentiful.
The framework covers five model classes:

Exponential growth: first-order ODE constraints, with theory for bias, variance and bandwidth selection
Quasi-exponential growth: growth rates that drift over time
General linear ODEs
General nonlinear ODEs, benchmarked against parameter-cascade (PCODE) methods
Second- and higher-order ODEs

Across these, the DE-constrained estimators achieve lower asymptotic bias than conventional local polynomial estimators of the same degree while keeping comparable variance, and they perform markedly better under sparse designs.

title: Research
text:
Applications


🔥 Fire science
Estimating burning-rate curves from firebrand data (Albini, 1979).


🦠 Epidemiology
SIR-based epidemic detection and reproduction-number estimation using Korean influenza-like-illness surveillance data.


🧬 Oncology
Tumour-growth curves from sparse longitudinal measurements.

title: Curve Estimation from Sparse Data
text:
My PhD work developed statistical methods that combine differential equations with local polynomial regression, so that curves can be estimated accurately even where data are sparse.
Highlights

Built a unified estimation framework covering exponential, quasi-exponential, linear, nonlinear and higher-order ODE models
Proved lower asymptotic bias than standard local polynomial estimators at comparable variance
Ran extensive simulation studies under uniform and sparse designs
Applied the methods to firebrand burning-rate data, Korean influenza surveillance data and tumour growth

Read more on the Research page →

title: Chunlei Ge
text:
Statistician & Data Scientist · PhD in Statistics, UBC Okanagan · Kelowna, BC
I am a statistician who builds models that stay reliable when data are messy, sparse or expensive to collect. I completed my PhD in Statistics at the University of British Columbia (Okanagan) in 2026, where my research combined differential equations with nonparametric regression to estimate growth and decay curves from limited data, with applications in fire science, epidemiology and oncology.
Alongside research, I spent several years as a graduate teaching assistant for mathematics, statistics and data courses, so I am used to explaining technical results to people who aren’t statisticians. I also hold an MA in Statistics from York University.
I’m looking for roles in statistics, data science and analytics where careful modelling makes a real difference to decisions.
